title: The lives behind the casualties
intro: The catalogue of kills repeatedly pauses over a victim’s special skill or family history. Divine favour, craftsmanship, and an affectionate upbringing cannot protect these men. The grammar alternates compressed battle formulas with relative clauses that briefly restore an individual life.

notes.text: αἵμων here means ‘skilled, knowledgeable,’ not ‘bloody’: the genitive θήρης specifies hunting as the sphere of expertise. θηρητῆρα is accusative singular of θηρητήρ, ‘hunter,’ in apposition to Scamandrius. The object of ἕλε stretches from line 49 into 51 before the explanation of his skill begins.

ἕλε is unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω, ‘slew.’ ὀξυόεντι is dative singular of ὀξυόεις, ‘sharp,’ agreeing with instrumental ἔγχεϊ. οὔρεσιν is epic dative plural of ὄρος, ‘mountain.’ ἄγρια πάντα means wild creatures generally; the relative τά refers back to this neuter plural object. ὕλη, ‘woodland,’ is subject of τρέφει.

χραῖσμε is an unaugmented aorist of χραισμέω, ‘avail, defend,’ with dative οἱ. Artemis’ title ἰοχέαιρα means ‘showering arrows.’ ἑκηβολίαι are long-distance shots; ᾗσιν is instrumental dative plural, ‘with which.’ ἐκέκαστο is pluperfect of καίνυμαι, ‘excel,’ with the sense ‘had distinguished himself.’ His former distinction now fails him.

ἕθεν is the epic third-person genitive pronoun, governed by πρόσθεν: ‘in front of him.’ φεύγοντα agrees with μιν, Scamandrius. οὔτασε is aorist of οὐτάω, ‘wound, thrust at.’ μετάφρενον supplies the place struck, the back; πρηνής describes his forward fall, ‘face down.’ The repeated armour-clatter formula links this death with the preceding page.

τέκτων is a skilled maker or carpenter, here genitive τέκτονος. Ἁρμονίδεω is an epic genitive of the patronymic Ἁρμονίδης. The clustered genitives and following ὅς make the family description compact; the narrative goes on to emphasize the craftsmanship associated with Phereclus. δαίδαλα are skilfully fashioned works, object of τεύχειν, ‘make,’ after ἐπίστατο, ‘knew how.’

ἐφίλατο is an aorist middle form from the φιλέω family, ‘loved, favoured’; its subject is Athena. τεκτήνατο is unaugmented aorist middle of τεκταίνομαι, ‘build, fashion.’ Ἀλεξάνδρῳ is the beneficiary: Alexander is Paris. νῆας ἐΐσας is ‘well-balanced / shapely ships’; ἐΐσας agrees with the accusative plural νῆας.

ἀρχέκακος means ‘beginning evil,’ an adjective applied to the ships that carried Paris on his disastrous expedition. οἷ is third-person dative, strengthened by αὐτῷ: ‘to himself too.’ The relative clause explicitly connects the craftsman’s own death with the larger Trojan catastrophe. This is narrative retrospect rather than merely a description of shipbuilding.

ᾔδη is an epic third-singular pluperfect of οἶδα, with past meaning ‘knew.’ θέσφατα are divine decrees or oracles, its object; ἐκ θεῶν means ‘from the gods,’ with the preposition placed after θεῶν. οὔ τι intensifies the denial, ‘not at all.’ The line does not spell out a particular oracle, so the note should not manufacture one.

κατέμαρπτε, from καταμάρπτω, means ‘caught up with’ as he pursued (διώκων). βεβλήκει is third-singular pluperfect active of βάλλω, here vividly recording the completed thrust. γλουτόν is the buttock, accusative of the body part struck. The subject then changes to ἀκωκή, ‘point,’ postponed to the end of line 67; ἣ anticipates it.

διαπρό and ἀντικρύ emphasize passage right through; κύστις is the bladder, and ὀστέον the bone. γνύξ is an adverb, ‘on the knees,’ not a declined noun here. ἔριπε is unaugmented second aorist of ἐρείπω. οἰμώξας, aorist participle of οἰμώζω, supplies the cry; death then ‘covered him all around,’ ἀμφεκάλυψε.

ἔπεφνε is a reduplicated aorist of the verb conventionally cited as πέφνω, ‘slay’; do not label it perfect solely because of πε-. νόθος marks birth outside the legitimate marriage. πύκα, literally ‘closely, firmly,’ here conveys careful nurture. Theano raised him ἶσα φίλοισι τέκεσσι, ‘equally with her own children’; φίλος can mean ‘one’s own.’

χαριζομένη is present middle participle of χαρίζομαι, ‘gratify,’ with dative πόσεϊ, an uncontracted form from πόσις, ‘husband.’ ᾧ is possessive ‘her own.’ Φυλεΐδης, ‘son of Phyleus,’ names Meges again by patronymic. ἐγγύθεν, ‘from close by,’ modifies his approach; ἰνίον is the nape, specified by genitive κεφαλῆς.

τάμε is unaugmented second aorist of τέμνω, ‘cut.’ χαλκός, the bronze weapon, is subject. ὀδόντας is accusative plural after ἀνά, while ὀδοῦσιν is dative plural of the same stem ὀδοντ-, here instrumental: he grips the cold bronze ‘with his teeth.’ The shift of case follows the weapon’s path into the final bodily image.
